issues.legal_issue: A general revisional power does not extend to an appellate order made by an officer exercising authority delegated by the government.
material_facts: A landholder challenged a repartition in consolidation proceedings and appealed to the State Government after an earlier appeal had failed.
An assistant director heard the appeal under authority delegated by the State Government and allowed it, changing the landholder’s allotment.
At another landholder’s request, the State Government used its revisional power to set aside the delegated appellate order and restore the original repartition.
issues.conclusion: By a 3–2 majority, the Court held that the State Government lacked jurisdiction to revise the delegated appellate order, and that the resulting order was a nullity. The dissenting judges considered the order revisable.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 21(4) and 41(1) of the East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948, an officer deciding an appeal under authority delegated by the State Government exercises the Government’s power, so the resulting order is an order of the Government. Section 42’s reference to an order passed by an officer under the Act covers an officer exercising independent statutory authority, not a delegate exercising the Government’s authority. The majority relied on the agency meaning of “delegate” in Huth v. Clarke, rejected the contrary interpretation in Lakha Singh v. Director, Consolidation of Holdings, Punjab, and distinguished the inference from legislative inaction discussed in Ramnandan Prasad Narayan Singh v. Mahanath Kapildeo Ram.

predicates.consolidation_proceeding: The dispute arose from proceedings to consolidate and repartition landholdings.
predicates.state_revision_challenges_delegated_appe: The State sought to revise an appellate order made by an officer acting under authority delegated to that officer by the State.
predicates.appeal_authority_belongs_to_state: The relevant appellate authority was conferred on the State, which authorized an officer to exercise it on its behalf.

issues.definition: When a consolidation dispute involves state revision of an appeal decided by an officer exercising the State’s delegated appellate authority, that appellate order is not subject to the State’s general revisional power.

issues.legal_issue: A serious and inevitable threat of deprivation of property caused by an unlawful state order can support constitutional relief before the deprivation occurs.
material_facts: The challenged state order restored a repartition that allotted the disputed plots to another landholder.
If the order stood, the other landholder could seek possession and the State would give effect to that allotment, leaving the petitioner unable to resist the transfer.
Possession had not yet been delivered, but the resulting loss of the petitioner’s property was considered inevitable if the order remained in force.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the threatened property deprivation was sufficient to affect the petitioner’s fundamental rights and permit relief under Article 32 without requiring the petitioner to wait for the deprivation to occur.
issues.legal_principle: Article 32 permits relief where an unlawful state order presents a sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental right. The Court treated the inevitable loss of property upon implementation of the order as a sufficient threat, even though possession had not yet changed hands.

predicates.constitutional_rights_petition: A person applied to the Supreme Court for relief against an alleged infringement of a fundamental right.
predicates.state_order_would_transfer_property_to_a: A state order, if implemented, would entitle another person to take possession of property claimed by the applicant.
predicates.resulting_property_loss_is_inevitable: The applicant would be unable to prevent the loss of the property if the state order were implemented.

issues.definition: If a constitutional rights petition challenges a state order that would transfer property to another holder and inevitably cause the applicant to lose it, a constitutional writ is available before the loss occurs.
